props.title: The Slumber Party Massacre
props.initialSlug: Teen slumber party turns into bloody power drill terror

sections.content: The Slumber Party Massacre (1982) stands as a fascinating subversion of slasher conventions, written by feminist activist Rita Mae Brown and directed by Amy Holden Jones. Unlike many exploitation films of the era, it deliberately plays with male gaze expectations, turning the drill-wielding killer into an obvious phallic symbol while giving its female characters genuine agency. This sits in stark contrast to contemporaries like Friday the 13th (1980) and Prom Night (1980), though it still delivers the expected genre thrills.

sections.content: The film launched a distinct wave of female-centered slashers that challenged genre norms while working within exploitation frameworks. Slumber Party Massacre II (1987) took an even more surreal approach, featuring a rockabilly killer with a guitar-drill hybrid weapon. Later entries like Jennifer's Body (2009) and A Girl Walks Home Alone at Night (2014) would continue this tradition of using horror tropes to explore feminist themes.

The practical effects and confined setting showcase the ingenuity of low-budget 80s horror. While Halloween (1978) established many slasher conventions, The Slumber Party Massacre demonstrates how Roger Corman's New World Pictures could produce effective genre films that still carried subversive messages. The film's legacy influenced later meta-horror like Scream (1996) and The Final Girls (2015). SUBHEAD: The Female Gaze in Horror

movies.title: The House on Sorority Row
movies.slug: Smart sorority sisters face off against a mysterious killer in this stylish slasher with giallo influences

sections.content: Director Amy Holden Jones brings a distinct female perspective to standard slasher elements. The camera often lingers on male bodies in ways that mirror typical exploitation film treatment of women, while the female characters display practical responses to danger. This approach influenced later female-directed horror like American Psycho (2000) and Pet Sematary (2019), showing how genre conventions could be redirected to serve feminist narratives.
